nameStory: The name 'dogwood' has a curious history that doesn't involve dogs at all! It likely comes from 'dag wood' or 'dagger wood,' referring to the tree's extremely hard, dense wood that was once carved into daggers, arrows, and other tools. The 'flowering' part is obvious once you see this tree's spectacular spring display of what look like four large white petals.
description: Flowering dogwood is a small to medium-sized tree that puts on one of spring's most beloved shows in New England forests. Growing 15-30 feet tall, it has a distinctive layered branching pattern that creates elegant horizontal tiers. What most people think are the tree's flowers are actually four large, creamy white bracts (modified leaves) that surround tiny clusters of actual flowers in the center. The smooth, oval leaves turn brilliant red-orange in fall, and the tree's puzzle-piece bark becomes more interesting with age.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Four large, creamy white bracts (not true petals) surround a cluster of tiny yellow-green flowers in the center. Each bract has a distinctive notched tip that looks like it was pinched. The bracts feel papery and slightly waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, oval leaves arranged in pairs along the branches (opposite arrangement). Run your finger along the leaf edge - it's completely smooth with no teeth. The leaves have prominent curved veins that follow the leaf's oval shape.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark breaks into small, square blocks that look like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. Young bark is smooth and gray, while older bark has a distinctive alligator-hide pattern that's rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Branches grow in distinct horizontal layers, creating a tiered or pagoda-like silhouette. This layered branching pattern is especially noticeable in winter and makes the tree easy to spot even from a distance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red, oval berries appear in clusters in late summer and fall. Each berry is about the size of a large pea and has a slightly bitter taste that birds love but humans should avoid.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are distinctive - flower buds are round and plump like tiny onions, while leaf buds are more pointed. Both are covered in what looks like overlapping scales and feel firm to gentle pressure.

habitat: Flowering dogwood thrives in the understory of mixed deciduous and coniferous forests throughout New England, preferring well-drained, slightly acidic soils. You'll often find it growing alongside maples, oaks, and hemlocks on gentle slopes and in protected valleys. It's also commonly planted in suburban yards and parks, where it can handle partial shade but blooms best with some morning sunlight.

seasonality.spring: The spectacular white bracts appear in late April to early May, just as the leaves begin to emerge. This is when the tree is most noticeable and easiest to identify from a distance.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed out with smooth, dark green foliage arranged in the characteristic tiered pattern. Small clusters of developing fruit begin to form where the spring bracts were.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of red, orange, and burgundy, while clusters of bright red berries ripen and attract birds. The fall color display rivals the spring flowering for sheer beauty.
seasonality.winter: The distinctive layered branching pattern and puzzle-piece bark make identification possible even without leaves. Plump flower buds are already visible, promising next spring's display.

funFact: Flowering dogwood wood is so incredibly hard and dense that it was once the preferred material for making textile mill shuttles, golf club heads, and even mallets - it's actually harder than oak and doesn't split easily when hammered repeatedly!
confusionNotes: The non-native kousa dogwood is increasingly common in landscaping and blooms about a month later than our native flowering dogwood. Remember: kousa has pointed bracts (like little caps) while flowering dogwood has notched, heart-shaped bracts. If the 'petals' look pinched at the tips, it's our native flowering dogwood!
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that the showy white 'petals' aren't actually petals at all, but modified leaves called bracts. The real flowers are the tiny yellow-green cluster in the center. This is similar to poinsettias, where the colorful parts are bracts, not flowers. Also, despite being called 'flowering' dogwood, all dogwoods produce flowers - this species just has the showiest display.
compareHints: Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size. Most other dogwoods are shrubs with small, white flower clusters - like red osier dogwood with its bright red winter stems, or gray dogwood with its white berries. The tiny Canadian bunchberry stays close to the ground with whorl-arranged leaves, while alternate-leaved dogwood is the only dogwood with leaves that alternate rather than growing in pairs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
